I'm Guy Martin, a security and infrastructure leader based in Dubai with 20+ years in IT.
Most recently I was VP of Information Security at ConnectWise. Before that I ran cloud engineering at Axcient: four datacenters, 10,000+ Linux VMs and hundreds of petabytes of storage. Earlier roles include Cisco TAC, network operations at the European Parliament and ethical hacking at PwC Luxembourg.
I've been an open source geek for as long as I've been in IT. I ported Gentoo to HPPA (PA-RISC), and since 2008 I've been building packet-o-matic, a real-time network forensics tool that turns live traffic into events and payloads. It evolved into pom-ng, and I'm now rewriting it in Rust as pktaddikt, an event-driven deep packet inspection engine, with experimental MCP support so AI agents can work with live network data. I presented Sniffing Cable Modems at DEF CON 16 in 2008 and HAR2009, and have also spoken at OHM.
These days I build and break things at home: local LLMs, AI agents, Linux and networking. This blog is where I write about my experiments.
Opinions are my own.
Contact

Email: blog@martin.ae

https://blog.martin.ae/local-llm-with-ol.body:
Running an agent with a local model on my own hardware: some notes
I wanted to try Hermes Agent, but I wanted to find out if I could have a fully local setup running.
The motivation was 2 fold: privacy, and cost. I'd like to keep everything local, I have nextcloud, fileserver and even my own mail server.
As for cost, if I can avoid spending $100 a month by using hardware I already have, that'd be a small win.
The setup
As a former Gentoo dev, I'm still faithful to the distro. I'm running it on all my machines. My workstation has 64GB of RAM and a RX6800 with 16GB VRAM.
I decided to install ollama on my workstation and hermes on a test VM to limit the blast in case it would go rogue.
Ollama was fairly easy to install, emerge ollama did the trick after I added USE=rocm in make.conf.
Finding the right model to run in ollama
First attempt: qwen2.5-coder:14b
After a quick search, qwen2.5-coder:14b appeared to be a good fit for my 16GB VRAM and intended use.
Deployment is very easy with ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:14b, it downloads the model and allows you to use it in minutes. However when connecting Hermes to ollama, I ran into the issue that this specific model only supports 32K context length and Hermes requires at least 64K.
Next attempt: gpt-oss:20b
That model is 13GB, not too bad to fit on my 16GB of VRAM. However, it wasn't very useful for the tasks I needed. It did work but it wasn't doing very well for tasks that required more thinking.
Sometimes, I was asking a question to the model and it was returning that question right back at me. Not very useful :)
Another attempt: qwen3.5:9b-q8_0
That model is smaller than gpt-oss:20b, it only uses 10GB. While it does fit in the VRAM, it wasn't very useful either.
Trying gemma4:31b
The recommended model for hermes is gemma4:31b. Unfortunately the model you can pull with ollama is too big for my VRAM. Running it would have ollama offload half of it on the CPU.
It made things very very slow and the system became unstable.
Trying to find an alternative, Claude suggested that I could use the same model but different quantization. This would keep the same model but reduce its size.
I attempted gemma4:31b Q3_K_M, while the file on hugging face is only 14GB, it would still not fit in my VRAM:
While the model is definitely more usable, it is still very slow. At least this model was able to use the MCP interface for my CRM Twenty. Previous model did not understand how to use it and were unable to list companies or contacts.
Next was gemma4:31b Q3_K_S, the file was slightly smaller but still not a win :
With more tweaking, using LLAMA_ARG_FIT_TARGET=0, I was able to reduce the offload to 19% but it still wasn't enough:
Time to reduce the quantization some more! Here comes IQ3_XXS !
Despite reducing the size of the model, it still didn't fit the VRAM :-/
Even with a bit of CPU offloading, things were really slow. At least this model was still able to use the tools correctly but it was too slow to be usable for daily use.
With Claude's advice, I tried gemma4:26B, it's not a dense model but a MoE (Mixture of Experts) model. It means that the CPU offloading shouldn't hurt as much since only some part of the model will be active at once.
It indeed wasn't too slow with the request, it was responding in a matter of seconds rather than minutes.
Unfortunately that model didn't prove to be very useful. Even if it was faster, it still felt very slow compared to Claude and it wasn't able to use some MCP, constantly failing to issue the proper command.
Takeaways
Unfortunately, running a local model is a tradeoff between speed and quality.
Despite many tweaks and attempts, I wasn't able to find a usable model.
A small model isn't anywhere near useful. It cannot use tools, provides very simple answers or doesn't understand the query.
Using a bigger model leads to a usable response but only if you are fine with waiting many minutes between answers. At a speed of 3-4t/s, you'll fall fast asleep.
I wanted to try this to limit the cost of my AI usage but it will slow me down more than anything else. Currently my AI use doesn't justify buying more powerful hardware.
I'll wait until the hardware price goes down or my AI usage cost goes significantly up :)

https://blog.martin.ae/local-llm-with-st.body:
Introduction
A week ago I started testing Strata. It gave great speed compared to ollama.
However there were a few bumps on the road to get something working well with Hermes agent.
I also wanted to see if I could get more out of it. Better model for better quality or faster speed.
The setup
AMD Radeon RX6800 (16GB VRAM)
64GB RAM DDR4
AMD Ryzen 7 5700G
Gentoo Linux
Model Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
Better models
I was running IQ2_XS but IQ3_XXS and IQ3_S are available.
Model tweaks
In order to improve quality, a few variables were changed to match Qwen's published guidance.
NameDefaultNew valueNote
temperature0 (greedy)0.6Introduce a bit of randomness in the next token to avoid loops
top_k6420Only the 20 most likely tokens can be picked
top_p10.95Keep candidates until their probability adds up to 95% and drop the rest
presence_penalty0 (off)1.5Any token that already appeared in the last 64 tokens gets a fixed penalty, however often it appeared; this is the main loop breaker
While these changes are great to avoid loops and get better results, they introduce a slight speed penalty.
Testing IQ3_S
Of course the first thing you do is test the best model. Well it didn't really work out well.
Although the README says that it fits, and it does, it doesn't leave enough room for essential things such as conversation cache.
The speed was 31-44t/s, so about 25% slower than the speed of IQ2_XS and even slower on longer prompts.
There is a low-RAM mode but things become even slower when I tested it. While reading prompts remained at the same speed in normal mode, it dropped to about 250-350 t/s in low-RAM mode.
This plus the fact that conversation cache did not have enough space meant that every single prompt needed to be fully re-read. It took several minutes for each request.
The low-RAM mode makes the kernel load the experts when needed instead of having dedicated RAM allocated for them.
There was a bit of quality increase in the responses. The answers were more detailed but it's all empirical and I don't really have a good way to measure this.
Testing IQ3_XXS
This model had the promise to use less memory. And it did. Compared to the ~50GB of experts in RAM for IQ3_S, IQ3_XXS uses ~42GB in RAM. That leaves 8GB more RAM for conversation cache.
This model is about 15% faster than IQ3_S and reading speed did not change. It's about 20% slower than IQ2_XS but quality seemed identical to IQ3_S.
Claude was testing the models by having them summarize Hamlet in about 300 words. Surprisingly, IQ3_XXS succeeded while IQ3_S failed half the time like IQ2_XS did.
Keep in mind that this was not a rigorous test so treat those results lightly. Always test with your own workflow.
The big advantage of this model is that it left enough room for the conversation cache. I could now have a couple sub agents running and the prompt reading would be fast.
Memory constraint
Firefox
In order to fit those bigger models, I had to reduce the memory as much as possible. Strata is running on my workstation and Firefox was the biggest memory user.
Updating those settings in about:config made Firefox unload the tabs I didn't need :
With this Firefox was now using less than 1GB of RAM instead of 10GB+. It did make some tabs slow when switching to them but unless it's a heavy tab you don't feel the difference.
Conversation cache
Strata caches the conversation so that it doesn't have to re-read most of the prompt. It continues from where the prompt was modified.
This is great if you keep reusing the context and adding more like in a session or conversation. However if you spawn sub agents, they will each have their own prompt and the cache will be lost at each run.
Lowering the free RAM floor in Strata to 1GB will tell it to save conversations in the cache until there is 1GB free. The default is 2.5GB.
Use --conversation-cache-min-free-mib 1024 to do so.
I settled on 4 slots and a total of 6GB conversation cache (for all slots). It fits the RAM and can keep big conversations in the cache. However the cache itself uses more RAM.
VRAM reserve
With a very light desktop running (awesomewm), Firefox was the main VRAM user. Reserving 2GB proved to be enough in my case: --vram-reserve-mib 2000.
Without this the system would freeze from time to time with the increased memory pressure on the VRAM.
General tweaks
There are a few other things I changed to improve stability and usability.
Upgrade Strata
The codebase was only 2 weeks old when I started testing. Since it's been released, it is under heavy development and new features are coming at a regular pace.
I've upgraded to 0.1.43.1. This improved some ROCm stability by pulling a known stable version. In my initial test run, the ROCm version pointed at by the setup was non existent and Claude pulled the latest one at the time. However it was not the best choice.
F16 arithmetic
By switching to F16 math using STRATA_HIP_PROMPT_F16=1, prompt reading is twice as fast! Where I was previously having 350-400t/s, I now achieve 700-800t/s for reading. This is a massive improvement especially for long prompts.
It helps as well when there is a cache miss with the conversation cache.
Minimum token count for cache insertion
Hermes and Claude both send small queries to Strata in order to generate titles or summaries. Those usually are one off. By setting --conversation-cache-min-tokens 8192, those queries don't make it into the cache and the long ones aren't discarded.
Hermes specific tweaks
Subagents issue
Since Strata runs one request at a time, each subagent has its request processed in turn and the context cache is lost. This is why the conversation cache tweak above was very important. Otherwise each sub agent doing their own request at each turn would just invalidate the previous cache and reading time goes through the roof.
I settled on allowing max 2 sub agents. That way one can be running a query with Strata while the other performs an action like a websearch. Strata supports multiple parallel queries and I tested that too. Keep reading.
Other changes in Hermes
Parallel queries processing
I tried parallel queries, it works but has speed penalties so I decided not to use it.
When enabled, you lose 10-25% speed compared to serialized queries. On top of that, when 2 queries run together, they run at 40% speed.
When limiting Hermes to 2 sub agents, it's not that often that both need to send queries at the same time. At least in my scenario, one is busy doing a web_search or using some other tool while the other is performing a query.
This means that the performance loss isn't worth it.
Conclusion
IQ2_XSIQ3_XXSIQ3_SIQ3_S low-RAM
Generation43–62 t/s36–49 t/s31–44 t/s26-41 t/s
Experts in RAM35.5 GB42.9 GB50.3 GBRead from disk when needed (not held in RAM)
Prompt reading694 t/s (6.2K), 749 t/s (25.6K)733 t/s (6.2K), 773 t/s (25.6K)727 t/s (6.2K), 733 t/s (25.6K)340 t/s (6.2K), 247 t/s (25.6K)
Cache fits✅ Yes (~10 GB free)⚠ Only with Firefox trimmed (~5–6 GB free)❌ No (~2 GB free, swapping)⚠ 4 GB cache worked, but swap grew from 6 to 12 GB (~5 GB free)
Hamlet summaryFinished 1/2 (304 words); the other reached token limit counting words✅ Finished 2/2 (298 and 301 words)Finished 1/2 (299 words); the other reached token limit counting wordsFinished 1/2 (299 words); the other reached token limit counting words
VerdictFastest and lightest; much better at temperature 0.6Best balance and most reliable output; RAM is tightNot enough RAM for the conversation cache; one GPU hang during testsReads prompts 2–3× slower, and the PC still swaps
IQ3_XXS offers the best balance in terms of quality, speed and actually fitting on my system. It meant lowering the RAM usage of other software running on my system to be able to run it.
With a lot of tweaking, I was able to achieve better quality although at a 20% speed reduction. There are a lot of parameters and understanding their impact is not always easy.
Testing is still the best thing you can do against your own workflow and usage.

https://blog.martin.ae/local-llm-with-st.body:
Trying to run a local LLM again but with Strata
My last attempt to run a local LLM with ollama on my workstation was a failure. Either the model was useless or too slow.
This week, a new backend for models showed up in hackernews: Strata.
It made bold claims. It should be able to run 40-50 token per second on hardware similar to mine. That is a RX6800 with 16GB VRAM and 64GB of system RAM.
I had to try it!
Installation
Installation was very easy. I went with the path of least resistance and pasted their prompt in claude:
After a few questions, minor hiccups that claude handled well and a hefty download, it was ready.
I settled on the model qwen3.8-flash-next-iq2_xs recommended for my setup.
How it works
Compared to ollama, Strata focuses on a single model which is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE). Each expert can be offloaded to either the GPU or the CPU.
Strata loads the important ones and the ones you use more often in the GPU and the rest in the CPU, allowing for very fast processing when it matters.
More details can be found here.
First attempt via the Web UI
I usually test models by asking for a joke. It's an easy answer and more often than not you get the one about physicists not trusting atoms.
For once I was given a joke in no time which made me laugh. Unfortunately I did not capture it.
The model felt blazing fast! A few more queries were answered very fast as well. You can see the thinking process in the UI which is set to high by default.
Looking at the monitor page, I was getting about 30-40t/s. Not great, not terrible.
Optimizing
Of course the first thing you want to do is get even more speed out of it!
First I used --vram-reserve-mib 1500. This gave me a bit of breathing room for my apps since this is my main workstation. This would not sound like an optimisation but relieving the pressure on the VRAM definitely helped.
With this change, my workstation was not hanging anymore and I consistently got around 40-50t/s.
I asked Claude for a bit of help and he pointed out that my graphic card was plugged in the wrong PCIe port. I moved it a while back to a lower 16x PCIe port because the nvme was underneath it and was getting too hot. After a lot of troubleshooting I think the issue is the sensor on the nvme and not the temperature itself. This is because PCIe ports aren't all wired the same. The top one on my motherboard is wired directly to the CPU and is a 16x one. The other one, while having a 16x slot, is only a 4x port and wired through the motherboard chipset, sharing the bandwidth with the other ports.
By moving the graphic card back to the right port, the PCIe bandwidth went from ~3GB/s to a whopping ~12GB/s. This helped a lot. I was now getting 50-60t/s!
Another small win is to enable --draft-vocab en. This prevents loading non-english languages and frees up a bit of VRAM allowing for more experts to load on the GPU. Gains were about 1%, not really measurable tho.
The model now felt very very fast and more than usable!
Tuning for hermes agent
First thing I did was increase the context window. I went from 64K to 128K without losing performance. This was amazing. I haven't tried 256K yet but performance are supposed to drop by ~20% doing so.
Hermes also requests the full context size each time so you have to set fix_max_tokens to true.
Enabling display.show_reasoning: true in hermes allows you to see the model thinking as well.
One useful thing to do as well is to enable api-monitor. This gives you a great view of the queries being performed as well as their output. Use with care if you share the instance!
Using it with hermes
Hermes now felt very useful. It managed to parse ods files, use the result to perform web searches and then give me a summary.
It was slower than Claude of course but the performances were amazing.
The cons
There are a few gotchas you need to be aware of.
First of all, it only processes one request at a time. Each request is queued and answered one by one. This is not a big deal but a request from hermes to summarize the conversation might delay your actual work.
This might be a problem as well with sub agents or if you share access with a team.
Secondly, if you restart it, the cache is lost. The first query with a huge context will take some time to load. Subsequent ones will be faster.
Conclusion
Strata makes local LLM a real possibility with consumer hardware. My workstation is about 5 years old and provides great results.
With my aging hardware I was able to get 50-60t/s on average.
